title: Extended and Altered Chords
intro: Keep stacking thirds above a seventh chord and you reach ninths, elevenths and thirteenths. Raise or lower those upper notes and you get altered chords. Together they give jazz, pop and late-Romantic music their colour.

blocks.text: Above the seventh come the 9th (a compound 2nd), the 11th (compound 4th) and the 13th (compound 6th). A thirteenth chord in theory holds all seven notes of a scale, so in practice some are left out:

items: Ninth chords: C9 = C E G B♭ D (dominant ninth); Cmaj9 = C E G B D; Cm9 = C E♭ G B♭ D.

Eleventh chords: over a major third the natural 11th clashes with the 3rd a ninth below, so on major and dominant chords it is usually raised (♯11, Lydian colour) or the 3rd is omitted. Cm11 (C E♭ G B♭ D F) is common and smooth.
Thirteenth chords: C13 = C E (G) B♭ D (F omitted) A; the 13th is usually voiced on top with the 5th and 11th left out.

blocks.text: Dominant chords take alterations of the 5th and 9th freely, because they resolve anyway: ♭9 and ♯9 (C7♭9 = C E G B♭ D♭), ♭5/♯11 and ♯5/♭13. 'C7alt' means a dominant with any of ♭9, ♯9, ♯11 and ♭13 and no natural 5th or 9th; it is played from the altered scale (7th mode of melodic minor).

widget.title: Extended and altered chords on C (left hand root, right hand upper notes)

items: sus4: the 3rd replaced by the 4th, C F G. In classical music a suspension resolves 4–3; in pop, Csus4 and Csus2 (C D G) often stand alone.
add9: a triad with a 9th but no 7th, C E G D. 6 chords: C6 = C E G A, Cm6 = C E♭ G A, the usual tonic chords in older jazz and swing.
Power chord (C5): root and fifth only, the basis of rock guitar (see the Guitar topic, coming soon).

blocks.text: Lead sheets name chords by root and suffix. The conventions vary between publishers, but the common ones are: C (major), Cm or C– (minor), C7 (dominant 7), Cmaj7, CM7 or CΔ7 (major 7), Cm7, Cø7 or Cm7♭5, C°7 or Cdim7, C+ or Caug, Csus4, C6, C9, C7♯9, and slash chords such as C/E (C major with E in the bass) or D/C (a D triad over a C bass, an upper-structure sound).

Pianists rarely play every note of an extended chord. A standard jazz left-hand voicing leaves out the root (the bassist plays it) and plays the 3rd and 7th plus one or two colour tones: for Dm9, F–A–C–E ('A' voicing) or C–E–F–A ('B' voicing). These rootless voicings, popularised by Bill Evans and Wynton Kelly, move with very little motion from chord to chord through a ii–V–I (see Jazz Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/jazz-harmony)).

blocks.title: Spell
blocks.text: Spell G13 (with the usual omissions) and E♭maj7♯11.
solution: G13: G B (D) F A (C omitted) E: G B F A E, usually with the 13th (E) on top.
E♭maj7: E♭ G B♭ D; ♯11 = A (E♭ to A♭ is an 11th; raised, A). E♭ G B♭ D A.
blocks.answer: G B F A E; E♭ G B♭ D A

blocks.title: Read the symbol
blocks.text: What notes are in F/A, and how is it different from Am7?
solution: F/A is an F major triad (F A C) with A in the bass: a first-inversion F chord. Am7 is A C E G; it shares A and C but has E and G instead of F.
blocks.answer: A F C (F major in first inversion)
